subjects.displayTitle: Unity and the oneness of humanity
subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh asks why God created everyone from the same dust, and answers at once: so that no one should exalt himself over another. All of human oneness unfolds from there. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá pictures humanity as one tree with many branches, a body whose finest nerves must assist one another, a garden whose beauty lies in its varied colours, and each image turns a fact about our origin into a duty toward the person beside us. Knowing that unity is good, he warns, is not enough; it must be worked for, in kindness across inherited divisions, in religion recovered as a source of fellowship, and in the patient widening of a united family into a united village, city and world. Paul’s body with its many members and the care owed to the least honoured [1], and the Qur’anic word that peoples and tribes exist so that they may come to know one another [2], keep the question alive across traditions. The way onward runs through interconnectedness and unity in diversity, and into the long labour of race unity and universal peace.

order.why: Begin with the images of one tree, one body and many interdependent members. The passages describe a shared origin and ask what that relationship requires in practice. Read the distinctions between physical association and spiritual fellowship, and the different meanings given to unity. Difference in function can contribute to a common life; exclusion and superiority injure it. How does a statement about what humanity is become a responsibility toward another person? Compare these images with the actual neighboring subjects of interconnectedness and unity in diversity. Their presence together invites inquiry without making every metaphysical account of oneness identical.

Since We have created you all from one same substance it is incumbent on you to be even as one soul, to walk with the same feet, eat with the same mouth and dwell in the same land, that from your inmost being, by your deeds and actions, the signs of oneness and the essence of detachment may be made manifest.

shortened: The teachings specialized in Baha'u'llah are addressed to humanity. He says, "Ye are all the leaves of one tree." He does not say, "Ye are the leaves of two trees: one divine, the other satanic." He has declared that each individual member of the human family is a leaf or branch upon the Adamic tree; that all are sheltered beneath the protecting mercy and providence of God; that all are the children of God, fruit upon the one tree of His love. God is equally compassionate and kind to all the leaves, branches and fruit of this tree.
Therefore, we must love mankind as His creatures, realizing that all are growing upon the tree of His mercy, servants of His omnipotent will and manifestations of His good pleasure.

order.why: A community that seeks to unite others must attend to its own relationships. The readings connect the Covenant with continuity, consultation with shared understanding, and reconciliation with effective service. Particular disputes, elections and warnings amid persecution belong to their historical settings. One letter explicitly distinguishes counsel offered in wisdom from an absolute command; another asks for inquiry when a meaning is disputed. How can free consultation coexist with humility and a willingness to act together? What would prompt reconciliation require? Read community unity alongside the wider obligation to humanity, rather than allowing concern for the group to eclipse care for others.

Should harmony of thought and absolute unity be nonexistent, that gathering shall be dispersed and that assembly be brought to naught.

They must become united on the principle of reality, forget all their dogmas and hold fast to one divine Reality. A union of all the Asiatic countries on such a basis of friendship and co-operation with all humanity will be welcomed by the Western nations. shortened: May the eyes be opened and the ears become attentive; may souls become resuscitated and consort together in the utmost harmony as recipients of the same light. May the light of love shine forth and illumine hearts, and may human lives be cemented and connected until all of us may find agreement and tranquillity beneath the same tabernacle and with the standard of the Most Great Peace above us move steadily onward.

shortened: Let there be no mistake. The principle of the Oneness of Mankind--the pivot round which all the teachings of Baha'u'llah revolve--is no mere outburst of ignorant emotionalism or an expression of vague and pious hope.... Its message is applicable not only to the individual, but concerns itself primarily with the nature of those essential relationships that must bind all the states and nations as members of one human family. It does not constitute merely the enunciation of an ideal, but stands inseparably associated with an institution adequate to embody its truth, demonstrate its validity, and perpetuate its influence.

questions: What do the images of tree, body, ocean and family each reveal about human oneness? Compare 1 Corinthians 12:12–27 and explore interconnectedness and unity in diversity. Where do their meanings overlap, and where do their religious settings or scope differ?

Which practices in these readings challenge racial, religious, national or class prejudice? Read Qur’an 49:13 alongside the passages on diversity and explore racial issues and slavery. How would recognition of equal dignity change a community’s habits and arrangements?

How do the passages test a claim to love by conduct? Compare practical assistance, the full reconciliation story and the distinction between knowing, intending and acting. What would it take to repair a particular relationship without overlooking justice?

How do consultation, the Covenant and prompt reconciliation contribute to community life? Compare instructions about disputed meanings, freedom in outward affairs and collective decisions. Which circumstances must be understood before applying a historical letter or reported conversation today?

What connects education, an auxiliary language, a house of worship, business practices and public communication? Explore universal language and community building. How could one of these institutions make mutual responsibility more effective while preserving diversity?

Compare the complete questions about protection with the supplied letters on stages of peace, then read a prayer for unity. What responsibilities and open questions remain for a community seeking to serve humanity?
